unit: Unit 14: Equations of Lines, Circles, and Conics
description: Write and convert equations of lines (slope-intercept, point-slope, standard); derive and apply equations of circles (center-radius form) and basic conics (parabolas; optional: ellipses/hyperbolas) for modeling and proof.
content:
Definitions

  • Linear Equation: An equation representing a straight line in the coordinate plane, generally written as y=mx+b.
  • Slope (m): The rate of change or steepness of a line, found by m=y2−y1x2−x1.
  • Y-Intercept (b): The point where the line crosses the y-axis (x=0).
  • X-Intercept: The point where the line crosses the x-axis (y=0).
  • Circle: The set of all points in a plane equidistant from a fixed point (the center). Standard form: (x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2.
  • Conic Sections: Curves obtained by slicing a cone: circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.

Key Concepts

  • Line Forms:
    • Slope-Intercept: y=mx+b.
    • Point-Slope: y−y1=m(x−x1).
    • Standard Form: Ax+By=C, where A, B, and C are integers.
  • Parallel Lines: Have equal slopes (m1=m2).
  • Perpendicular Lines: Slopes are negative reciprocals (m1·m2=−1).
  • Circle Equation Derivation: From distance formula: (x−h)2+(y−k)2=r → square both sides.
  • General Form of Circle: x2+y2+Dx+Ey+F=0.
  • Conic Types:
    • Circle: A=B, both positive.
    • Ellipse: A and B positive, unequal.
    • Parabola: Only one squared term.
    • Hyperbola: Coefficients of squared terms have opposite signs.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Lines)

  1. Identify given data: Slope, point(s), or intercepts.
  2. Select the correct form: Use point-slope if a point and slope are known; slope-intercept if the y-intercept is known.
  3. Substitute and simplify to desired form.
  4. Convert to standard form if integer coefficients are needed.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Circles)

  1. Identify center (h,k) and radius r.
  2. Substitute into standard form (x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2.
  3. Expand and simplify to obtain general form if needed.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Conics)

  1. Identify squared terms and signs to classify the conic.
  2. Complete the square when converting from general to standard form.
  3. Use the standard equation to find center, radius, vertices, or focus.

Example 1 — Equation of a Line

Given: Passes through (2, 3) with slope 4. Find equation.

  • Point-slope form: y−3=4(x−2).
  • Simplify: y=4x−5.

Example 2 — Equation of a Circle

Given: Center (−3, 4) and radius 5.

  • Standard form: (x+3)2+(y−4)2=25.

Example 3 — Classifying Conic Sections

Given: 9x2+16y2=144.

  • Both squared terms positive and unequal → Ellipse.
  • Divide by 144 to get standard form: x216+y29=1.

Example 4 — Completing the Square for Circle

Given: x2+y2+6x−4y−12=0. Find center and radius.

  • Group and complete squares: (x+3)2+(y−2)2=25.
  • Center (−3, 2), radius 5.

Example 5 — Parabola Identification

Given: y=114x2. Determine direction and vertex.

  • Equation matches y=ax2 → vertex at origin, opens upward.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always simplify fractions in slope calculations.
  • Check signs when using slope formulas — y-change over x-change.
  • Parallel lines → same slope, different intercepts; perpendicular → negative reciprocal slopes.
  • For circles, coefficients of x2 and y2 must be equal in sign and magnitude.
  • In conics, always bring to standard form to identify the type correctly.

unit: Unit 15: Reflections, Rotations, and Translations
description: Perform and describe reflections, rotations, and translations in the plane; determine orientation, distance, and angle preservation; use coordinate rules and matrices to represent transformations; verify congruence via rigid motions.
content:
Definitions

  • Rigid Motion (Isometry): A transformation that preserves distance and angle measure (figures remain congruent).
  • Translation: A slide that moves every point the same vector ⟨a,b⟩; rule: (x,y)→(x+a,y+b).
  • Reflection: A flip across a line (line of reflection); each point and its image are symmetric about the line and are equidistant from it.
  • Rotation: A turn about a center by a specified angle and direction (counterclockwise is positive).
  • Line Symmetry: A figure has line (mirror) symmetry if a reflection across some line maps the figure onto itself.
  • Rotational Symmetry: A figure matches itself after a rotation by an angle less than 360°; the smallest such angle is the angle of rotational symmetry.
  • Orientation: The order (clockwise/counterclockwise) of labeled vertices. Translations and rotations preserve orientation; reflections reverse it.

Key Concepts

  • Coordinate Rules (about the origin):
    • Translation T⟨a,b⟩: (x,y)→(x+a,y+b).
    • Reflection across x-axis: (x,y)→(x,−y); across y-axis: (x,y)→(−x,y).
    • Reflection across y=x: (x,y)→(y,x); across y=−x: (x,y)→(−y,−x).
    • Rotation 90° CCW: (x,y)→(−y,x); 180°: (x,y)→(−x,−y); 270° CCW: (x,y)→(y,−x).
  • Composition of Rigid Motions: The composition of isometries is an isometry (congruence mapping). Many compositions can be described as a single translation or rotation.
  • Mapping Under Reflections: A point on the line of reflection is invariant (maps to itself).
  • Symmetry Tests: A line of symmetry divides a figure into two congruent mirror halves; a figure with n-fold rotational symmetry maps to itself after rotation by 360n°.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Translations)

  1. Identify the vector ⟨a,b⟩.
  2. Add a to each x-coordinate and add b to each y-coordinate.
  3. Connect images in the same order; side lengths and angles are preserved.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Reflections)

  1. Choose the mirror (axis, y=x, or a general line).
  2. Use a rule for common mirrors (axes, y=x, y=−x), or construct a perpendicular from the point to the line and go the same distance on the other side.
  3. Check distances to the line are equal and the segment between a point and its image is perpendicular to the mirror.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Rotations about the Origin)

  1. Select angle (90°, 180°, 270° CCW) and apply the corresponding coordinate rule.
  2. For other angles, use rotation matrices or geometry tools; distances from the center remain constant.
  3. Verify orientation (translations/rotations preserve, reflections reverse).

Example 1 — Translate a Triangle

Given: A(−2,1), B(1,4), C(3,0). Translate by ⟨5,−3⟩.

  • Images: A'(3,−2), B'(6,1), C'(8,−3).

Example 2 — Reflect Across y=x

Given: P(4,−7). Find its image.

  • Rule: swap coordinates → P'(−7,4).

Example 3 — Rotate 90° CCW About Origin

Given: Q(6,2). Find Q'.

  • Rule: (x,y)→(−y,x) → Q'(−2,6).

Example 4 — Line Symmetry & Orientation

Given: Triangle △ABC reflected across the x-axis to △A'B'C'. Compare perimeters and orientation.

  • Perimeters equal (isometry). Orientation reverses: order A→B→C becomes clockwise vs. counterclockwise.

Example 5 — General Reflection Across y=2

Given: Reflect R(1,−3) across the horizontal line y=2.

  • Vertical distance to line is 5; reflect to the other side: R'(1,7).

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Keep vertex labels in order—orientation helps detect reflections vs. rotations/translations.
  • For reflections across non-axial lines (e.g., y=mx+b): translate/rotate to an axis, reflect using a rule, then undo the moves.
  • Distances from a line of reflection are equal; distances from a center of rotation are preserved.
  • Compositions: two reflections across parallel lines → a translation; across intersecting lines → a rotation (angle twice the angle between lines).
  • Symmetry check: try a suspected line/rotation and test whether key points map onto the figure.

unit: Unit 16: Glide Reflections and Compositions of Transformations
description: Compose multiple rigid motions and analyze the resulting single transformation (e.g., rotation as two reflections; translation as two reflections); define and construct glide reflections; prove properties using transformational geometry.
content:
Definitions

  • Isometry (Rigid Motion): A transformation that preserves distances and angle measures; images are congruent to preimages.
  • Composition of Transformations: Applying one transformation after another; order matters (generally noncommutative).
  • Glide Reflection: A composition of a reflection across a line ℓ followed by a nonzero translation parallel to ℓ. Rule example (across x-axis, then translate by ⟨a,0⟩): (x,y)→(x+a,−y).
  • Fixed Point: A point that maps to itself under a transformation. Reflections fix points on the mirror line; nontrivial glide reflections have no fixed points.
  • Orientation: Clockwise/counterclockwise order of labeled vertices. Reflections and glide reflections reverse orientation; translations and rotations preserve it.

Key Concepts

  • Order Matters: In general, F∘G ≠ G∘F. A reflection followed by a translation parallel to the mirror gives a glide reflection; reversing the order may change the mirror’s location.
  • Composing Reflections:
    • Across parallel lines distance d apart → a translation perpendicular to the lines with magnitude 2d.
    • Across intersecting lines with angle θ → a rotation by 2θ about the intersection.
  • Composing Translations: The result is a translation by the vector sum.
  • Reflection ∘ Translation (parallel to mirror): A glide reflection with the same mirror line and the given translation.
  • Symmetry: A figure has glide-reflection symmetry if some glide reflection maps it onto itself (common in frieze patterns, footprints).

Step-by-Step Procedure (Constructing a Glide Reflection)

  1. Choose the mirror line ℓ and the translation vector parallel to ℓ (e.g., for x-axis, use ⟨a,0⟩).
  2. Reflect the figure across ℓ.
  3. Translate the reflected image by the given vector (parallel to ℓ).
  4. Check orientation is reversed and distances/angles are preserved; verify no fixed points unless the vector is zero.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Reducing a Composition)

  1. Identify components (R = reflection, T = translation, Rot = rotation) and their order.
  2. Use identities:
    • R∘R (parallel) → translation by 2d.
    • R∘R (intersecting) → rotation by 2θ.
    • R∘T with T parallel to mirror → glide reflection.
    • T∘T → single translation (vector sum).
  3. Simplify to one isometry when possible (T, Rot, R, or glide reflection).

Example 1 — Coordinate Glide Reflection (Across x-axis)

Given: Reflect across the x-axis, then translate by ⟨6,0⟩. Find the image of P(−2,5).

  • Reflect: (−2,5)→(−2,−5); then translate: (−2,−5)→(4,−5).

Example 2 — Two Reflections Across Parallel Lines

Given: Reflect across lines y=1 and then y=4. Describe the single transformation.

  • Lines are parallel, distance d=3. Result is a translation by 2d=6 units perpendicular to the lines (upward).

Example 3 — Two Reflections Across Intersecting Lines

Given: Reflect across lines that meet at angle 30°. Describe the result.

  • Composition is a rotation by 60° about the intersection point.

Example 4 — Identify Orientation & Fixed Points

Given: A transformation maps triangle △ABC to △A'B'C', reversing vertex order and having no fixed points. What type is it?

  • Orientation reversing and no fixed points → glide reflection (not a pure reflection, which fixes the mirror line).

Example 5 — Noncommutativity

Given: Compare reflect across y=0 then translate by ⟨4,0⟩ versus translate then reflect.

  • First order (R then T) gives glide rule: (x,y)→(x+4,−y). Second order (T then R): (x,y)→(x+4,−y) (same here because the translation is parallel to the mirror); but for nonparallel cases, the mirror position changes → generally not the same mapping.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Glide reflection = reflection + parallel translation (nonzero). If the vector is zero, it’s just a reflection.
  • Two reflections: parallel lines → translation (by twice the distance); intersecting lines → rotation (twice the angle).
  • Track orientation: if it flips and there are no fixed points, suspect a glide reflection.
  • When reducing compositions, sketch intermediate images and annotate vectors/angles—this prevents order mistakes.
  • Vector sums combine translations; use coordinate rules to verify final images quickly.

unit: Unit 17: Symmetry and Tessellations
description: Identify and classify lines of symmetry and centers of rotational symmetry; analyze symmetry groups of plane figures and patterns; construct and justify tessellations (regular, semi-regular, and with transformations) and relate to angle measures.
content:
Unit 17: Symmetry and Tessellations

Objectives

  • Identify and classify lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry, and point symmetry in 2D figures.
  • Describe plane isometries (reflections, rotations, translations, glide reflections) and how they generate patterns.
  • Determine whether a polygon (regular or not) can tessellate the plane and justify using angle sums around a point.
  • Construct (by description) regular and semi-regular tessellations and record vertex configurations.

Key Definitions

  • Symmetry: A transformation that maps a figure onto itself.
  • Line (Axis) of Symmetry: A line that reflects a figure onto itself.
  • Rotational Symmetry: A figure has order n if a rotation by 360n° or less maps it onto itself; the angle of rotation is 360n°.
  • Point (Origin) Symmetry: A half-turn (180°) maps the figure onto itself.
  • Isometry: Distance-preserving transformation: reflection, rotation, translation, or glide reflection.
  • Tessellation (Tiling): A covering of the plane with no gaps or overlaps using one or more shapes (tiles).
  • Regular Tessellation: Uses one type of regular polygon; denotes by {n}.
  • Semi-Regular Tessellation: Uses two or more types of regular polygons with the same arrangement at each vertex; denote by vertex configuration (e.g., 3.3.3.4.4).
  • Vertex Configuration: Cyclic list of the number of sides of the polygons that meet at a point; the interior-angle sum there is 360°.

Facts and Tests

  • Interior Angle of Regular n-gon: (n−2)180n°.
  • Regular Tessellation Condition: A regular n-gon tessellates iff its interior angle divides 360°. Hence only equilateral triangles {3}, squares {4}, and regular hexagons {6} tessellate the plane.
  • Vertex-Sum Test (general): For any tiling, the sum of interior angles of tiles meeting at one vertex equals 360°.
  • Symmetry Orders (common figures): Equilateral triangle: order 3; square: order 4; regular n-gon: order n. A rectangle (non-square) has 2 lines of symmetry? No, it has 2 reflection lines only if it is a square; otherwise, a rectangle has 2 lines (through mid-segments) and order 2 rotation.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Identify Lines of Symmetry
    1. Look for mirrored halves across candidate lines (vertical, horizontal, diagonals).
    2. Fold-test mentally: would a reflection across the line match all points?
    3. State the number of distinct symmetry lines.
  2. Find Rotational Symmetry
    1. Rotate the figure around its center; find the smallest positive angle mapping it onto itself.
    2. Compute order n=360θ, where θ is that angle.
  3. Tessellation Feasibility (Regular)
    1. Compute a regular polygon’s interior angle α.
    2. Check if 360α is a whole number; if yes, it tessellates.
  4. Vertex Configuration (Semi-Regular)
    1. List polygons around one vertex (in order) as a dot-separated string, e.g., 3.4.6.4.
    2. Verify the interior-angle sum is 360°.
  5. Build a Tessellation (Translation Method)
    1. Start with a square (or triangle/hexagon). Cut a shape from one side.
    2. Translate that cut-out to the opposite side; repeat across the plane.
    3. Optionally add reflections/rotations to create symmetry variety.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Rotational Symmetry Order

Given: Regular octagon. Find: angle of rotation and order.

  • Angle of rotation: 3608=45°; order: 8.

Example 2 — Can a Regular Pentagon Tessellate?

Given: Regular pentagon (n=5). Decide: tessellates?

  • Interior angle: (5−2)1805=108°. Since 360108 is not an integer, a regular pentagon alone does not tessellate the plane.

Example 3 — Regular Tessellators

Claim: Only {3}, {4}, {6} tessellate.

  • Triangle: interior angle 60°; six meet at a point (6·60=360).
  • Square: interior angle 90°; four meet (4·90=360).
  • Hexagon: interior angle 120°; three meet (3·120=360).

Example 4 — Semi-Regular Tessellation Check

Given: Vertex configuration 3.3.3.4.4. Verify: tessellates?

  • Angles: triangle 60° (×3) and square 90° (×2). Sum 3·60+2·90=360° → valid semi-regular tiling.

Example 5 — Counting Symmetries

Given: A non-square rectangle. Find: all symmetries.

  • Reflections: across the lines through midpoints parallel to sides (2 lines).
  • Rotations: order 2 (rotation by 180° only). No diagonal reflections unless it is a square.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • For rotational symmetry, always report both the order and the smallest angle.
  • Use the vertex-sum test: interior angles meeting at a point must total 360°.
  • Regular pentagons alone do not tessellate; mixing shapes can fix the angle sum (semi-regular).
  • Isometries preserve lengths and angles—tiles remain congruent after reflections/rotations/translations.
  • Label a tessellation locally with its vertex configuration to communicate structure quickly.

unit: Unit 18: Area of Polygons and Circles
description: Calculate area of triangles, parallelograms, trapezoids, regular polygons (using apothem), and composite figures; apply the formula for the area of a circle and sectors; solve problems involving perimeter/circumference and area relationships.
content:
Unit 18: Area of Polygons and Circles

Objectives

  • Calculate the area of triangles, quadrilaterals, regular polygons, and circles using appropriate formulas.
  • Apply the area formulas to composite and shaded figures by decomposition and subtraction.
  • Derive and justify formulas for regular polygons and circles using apothem, radius, or sector relationships.

Key Definitions

  • Area: The amount of space enclosed within a two-dimensional shape, measured in square units.
  • Base and Height: In a polygon, the base is any side, and the height is the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex or side.
  • Apothem: The perpendicular distance from the center of a regular polygon to one of its sides.
  • Radius: The distance from the center of a circle to any point on its circumference.
  • Diameter: Twice the radius; the longest chord through the center of a circle.
  • Sector: A region of a circle bounded by two radii and the intercepted arc.
  • Composite Figure: A figure made up of two or more simple geometric shapes.

Formulas

  • Rectangle: A=bh
  • Square: A=s2
  • Parallelogram: A=bh
  • Triangle: A=12bh
  • Trapezoid: A=12(b1+b2)h
  • Rhombus/Kite: A=12d1d2
  • Regular Polygon: A=12aP, where a is the apothem and P is the perimeter.
  • Circle: A=πr2
  • Sector of Circle: A=θ360πr2

Concept Connections

  • All area formulas for polygons can be derived from 12bh (triangle area), since polygons can be decomposed into triangles.
  • For regular polygons, P=ns (where s is side length), and the apothem acts as height of each congruent isosceles triangle.
  • Area of a circle parallels that of a regular polygon with many sides: A=12aP becomes πr2 as n → ∞.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Find Area of a Regular Polygon
    1. Find the perimeter (P=ns).
    2. Find the apothem using trigonometry: a=s2÷tan(180n).
    3. Compute area: A=12aP.
  2. Find Area of Composite Figures
    1. Decompose into known shapes (rectangles, triangles, circles, etc.).
    2. Find area of each shape using its formula.
    3. Add or subtract as needed to match the shaded region.
  3. Find Area of a Sector
    1. Identify radius and central angle θ.
    2. Use formula A=θ360πr2.
    3. If arc length s is known, use A=r2s/2.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Area of a Regular Hexagon

Given: Side length = 6 cm. Find: Area.

  • P=6×6=36 cm.
  • a=62÷tan(30°)=5.196 cm.
  • A=12(5.196×36)=93.5 cm².

Example 2 — Area of a Sector

Given: Circle with radius 10 cm and central angle 90°.

  • A=90360π102=14π100=25π cm².

Example 3 — Composite Figure

Given: A rectangle (10 m × 6 m) with a semicircle of diameter 6 m attached on one side. Find: Area.

  • Rectangle: A=10×6=60 m².
  • Semicircle: A=12π32=4.5π ≈ 14.14 m².
  • Total: A=74.14 m².

Example 4 — Area of a Triangle (Given Coordinates)

Given: Vertices A(2, 1), B(8, 3), C(5, 7). Find: Area using coordinate formula.

  • A=12|2(3−7)+8(7−1)+5(1−3)|=12|−8+48−10|=15 units².

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always use perpendicular height, not slant height, when applying A=bh.
  • Check that all dimensions use the same unit before computing area.
  • Composite figures may require subtracting the inner unshaded part from the outer region.
  • For regular polygons, memorize A=12aP — it’s universal for all n.
  • For circles, radius squared grows faster than diameter — doubling radius quadruples area.
  • When approximating π, use 3.14 or fraction 227 for exactness preference.

unit: Unit 19: Surface Area of Solids
description: Find surface area of right prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres; decompose nets and apply lateral/total surface area formulas; solve real-world problems including composite solids and unit conversions.
content:
Definitions

  • Solid (3D Figure): A three-dimensional geometric shape that has volume and surface area.
  • Face: A flat surface on a solid.
  • Edge: A line segment where two faces meet.
  • Vertex: A point where edges meet.
  • Surface Area (SA): The total area of all the faces (or curved surfaces) that enclose a solid.
  • Lateral Area (LA): The sum of the areas of the faces excluding the bases.
  • Total Surface Area (TSA): The sum of the lateral area and the areas of the bases: TSA = LA + 2B.

Key Formulas

  • Prism: SA = 2B + Ph, where B is the area of the base, P is the perimeter of the base, and h is the height.
  • Cylinder: SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
  • Pyramid: SA = B + ½Pl, where l is the slant height.
  • Cone: SA = πr² + πrl.
  • Sphere: SA = 4πr².

Step-by-Step Procedures

1. Prisms

  1. Find the area of one base (B).
  2. Find the perimeter of the base (P).
  3. Multiply P by the height h for the lateral area (LA).
  4. Add 2B for total surface area.

2. Cylinders

  1. Compute area of the two circular bases: 2πr².
  2. Compute the lateral area (rectangle wrapped around the side): 2πrh.
  3. Add both to get SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.

3. Pyramids

  1. Find area of base (B).
  2. Find slant height (l).
  3. Compute lateral area (½Pl).
  4. Add base area for total surface area: SA = B + ½Pl.

4. Cones

  1. Find radius r and slant height l.
  2. Find base area: <πr²>.
  3. Find lateral area: <πrl>.
  4. Add to get SA = πr² + πrl.

5. Spheres

  1. Use formula SA = 4πr².
  2. Remember that the surface area grows with the square of the radius.

Example Problems

Example 1 — Surface Area of a Rectangular Prism

Given: Length = 8 cm, Width = 5 cm, Height = 3 cm.

  • SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)
  • SA = 2(8×5 + 8×3 + 5×3) = 2(40 + 24 + 15) = 158 cm²

Example 2 — Surface Area of a Cylinder

Given: Radius = 4 in, Height = 10 in.

  • SA = 2πr² + 2πrh
  • SA = 2π(4²) + 2π(4)(10) = 32π + 80π = 112π ≈ 351.9 in²

Example 3 — Surface Area of a Cone

Given: Radius = 3 cm, Slant height = 5 cm.

  • SA = πr² + πrl
  • SA = π(3²) + π(3)(5) = 9π + 15π = 24π ≈ 75.4 cm²

Example 4 — Surface Area of a Sphere

Given: Radius = 7 cm.

  • SA = 4πr² = 4π(7²) = 196π ≈ 615.8 cm²

Example 5 — Surface Area of a Square Pyramid

Given: Base side = 6 m, Slant height = 5 m.

  • B = 6² = 36; P = 4×6 = 24
  • SA = B + ½Pl = 36 + ½(24)(5) = 36 + 60 = 96 m²

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always include both bases when calculating total surface area (for prisms and cylinders).
  • Use slant height (l) for cones and pyramids, not vertical height.
  • Label units carefully — surface area is in square units.
  • Visualize nets (unfolded solids) to ensure all faces are counted.
  • Round answers only at the end to avoid compounding rounding errors.

unit: Unit 20: Volume of Prisms, Cylinders, Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres
description: Compute volumes of right prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres (and hemispheres); apply Cavalieri’s principle and volume relationships (e.g., pyramid/cone vs. prism/cylinder); solve modeling problems with composite figures.
content:
Definitions

  • Volume: The amount of 3D space a solid occupies; measured in cubic units.
  • Base (of a solid): The face (or region) used to generate the solid; its area is denoted B.
  • Height: The perpendicular distance between bases (for prisms/cylinders) or from the vertex to the base (for pyramids/cones); denoted h.
  • Slant Height: The lateral edge height for cones/pyramids (used for surface area, not for volume).
  • Right vs. Oblique: A solid is right if the height is perpendicular to the base; otherwise it is oblique. (Cavalieri's Principle ensures many volume formulas still hold.)

Key Formulas

  • Prism: V=Bh.
  • Cylinder: V=Bh with B=πr2 ⇒ V=πr2h.
  • Pyramid: V=13Bh.
  • Cone: V=13πr2h.
  • Sphere: V=43πr3.
  • Composite Solid: Add/subtract volumes of simpler parts (ensure overlapping regions are not double-counted).

Step-by-Step Procedure (General)

  1. Identify the solid and write the appropriate volume formula.
  2. Compute the base area B if needed (e.g., rectangle, triangle, regular polygon, or circle).
  3. Use the perpendicular height h (not the slant height for pyramids/cones).
  4. Substitute and simplify, keeping exact forms with π when appropriate; round only at the end.
  5. State units in cubic measure (e.g., cm3, in3).

Step-by-Step Procedure (By Solid)

  1. Prism: Find B of the base shape; multiply by height h.
  2. Cylinder: Compute B=πr2; multiply by h.
  3. Pyramid: Compute base area B; apply 13Bh.
  4. Cone: Use 13πr2h with perpendicular height (not slant).
  5. Sphere: Apply 43πr3.

Example 1 — Rectangular Prism

Given: l = 9 cm, w = 4 cm, h = 5 cm. Find volume.

  • Base area B=lw=9·4=36 cm2.
  • V=Bh=36·5=180 cm3.

Example 2 — Right Circular Cylinder

Given: r = 3 in, h = 12 in. Find volume.

  • V=πr2h=π·32·12=π·9·12=108π in3 (≈ 339.3 in3).

Example 3 — Square Pyramid

Given: Base side 10 m, height 15 m. Find volume.

  • Base area: B=102=100 m2.
  • V=13Bh=13·100·15=500 m3.

Example 4 — Right Cone

Given: Radius 6 cm, height 8 cm. Find volume.

  • V=13πr2h=13·π·62·8=13·π·36·8=96π cm3 (≈ 301.6 cm3).

Example 5 — Sphere

Given: Radius 5 ft. Find volume.

  • V=43πr3=43π·53=43π·125=5003π ft3 (≈ 523.6 ft3).

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Use perpendicular height for volume. Slant height appears in surface area, not volume.
  • For cylinders/cones, confirm the radius is to the center; diameter d means r=d2.
  • Keep π symbolic until the last step for exact answers; round only at the end.
  • Composite solids: add volumes of parts; subtract holes (e.g., cylinder with a cylindrical bore).
  • Units must be cubic; check that base area units times height units produce volume units.

unit: Unit 21: Special Right Triangles
description: Explore relationships in 45°–45°–90° and 30°–60°–90° triangles; derive and apply side ratios to find missing sides; solve geometric and real-world problems involving special right triangles and their properties.
content:
Definitions

  • Special Right Triangles: Right triangles with predictable ratios of side lengths, derived from geometric properties of squares and equilateral triangles.
  • 45°–45°–90° Triangle: An isosceles right triangle with both legs congruent and hypotenuse √2 times a leg.
  • 30°–60°–90° Triangle: A right triangle derived from an equilateral triangle cut in half; side ratios follow 1 : √3 : 2.
  • Leg: The sides adjacent to the right angle.
  • Hypotenuse: The side opposite the right angle; the longest side.

Key Ratios and Formulas

  • 45°–45°–90° Triangle:
    • If each leg = x, then hypotenuse = x2.
    • Conversely, if hypotenuse = h, each leg = h2.
  • 30°–60°–90° Triangle:
    • Short leg (opposite 30°) = x.
    • Long leg (opposite 60°) = x3.
    • Hypotenuse = 2x.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Solving for Missing Sides)

  1. Identify the triangle type (45–45–90 or 30–60–90) based on given angles or side relationships.
  2. Label the known side (leg or hypotenuse).
  3. Apply the ratio corresponding to the triangle type to find missing sides.
  4. Substitute the given value and simplify radicals as needed.
  5. Check that results are consistent with triangle side ordering (hypotenuse longest).

Example 1 — 45°–45°–90° Triangle

Given: Each leg = 7 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

  • h=x2 → h=72 cm ≈ 9.9 cm.

Example 2 — Reverse 45°–45°–90°

Given: Hypotenuse = 10 m. Find each leg.

  • x=h2 → x=102 ≈ 7.07 m.

Example 3 — 30°–60°–90° Triangle (Short Leg Given)

Given: Short leg = 5 in. Find the other sides.

  • Long leg = x3 → 53 ≈ 8.66 in.
  • Hypotenuse = 2x → 10 in.

Example 4 — 30°–60°–90° Triangle (Hypotenuse Given)

Given: Hypotenuse = 12 cm. Find the short and long legs.

  • Short leg = h2 = 6 cm.
  • Long leg = 63 ≈ 10.39 cm.

Example 5 — Mixed Problem

Given: A right triangle has one leg 9 m and an acute angle of 30°. Find the other sides.

  • Short leg = 9 m (opposite 30°).
  • Hypotenuse = 2x → 18 m.
  • Long leg = x3 → 93 ≈ 15.6 m.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Remember which side is opposite each angle — label before solving.
  • Never confuse the short and long legs in a 30°–60°–90° triangle: the longer side is opposite the 60° angle.
  • Use radical forms (e.g., 2, 3) exactly in symbolic answers unless instructed to approximate.
  • For coordinate geometry, the ratios hold regardless of triangle size — scaling multiplies all sides equally.
  • Verify hypotenuse > legs for correctness; if not, a computation error likely occurred.

unit: Unit 22: Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse
description: Apply and prove the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse; use it to determine triangle types and solve for unknown sides; apply to coordinate geometry and real-world distance problems in two and three dimensions.
content:
Unit 22: Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse

Objectives

  • Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find unknown side lengths in right triangles and in coordinate geometry.
  • Use the Converse of the Pythagorean Theorem to determine whether a triangle is right.
  • Recognize and generate Pythagorean triples; simplify radical lengths exactly.
  • Use Pythagorean inequalities to classify triangles as acute or obtuse.

Key Definitions

  • Right Triangle: A triangle with one 90° angle. The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse (length c); the other two sides are legs (lengths a, b).
  • Pythagorean Theorem: In a right triangle, a2+b2=c2.
  • Converse: If for a triangle with side lengths a, b, c (largest) we have a2+b2=c2, then the triangle is right with hypotenuse c.
  • Pythagorean Triples: Integer solutions to a2+b2=c2, e.g., 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17. Scalar multiples also work (e.g., 6-8-10).
  • Pythagorean Inequalities: For sides with c the largest: if a2+b2>c2 the triangle is acute; if a2+b2<c2 it is obtuse.

Core Formulas & Connections

  • Right Triangle: a2+b2=c2.
  • Distance in the Coordinate Plane: For points P(x1,y1), Q(x2,y2), d=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2 (derived from the theorem).
  • Special Right Triangles: 45-45-90: legs s, hypotenuse s2. 30-60-90: short leg s, long leg s3, hypotenuse 2s.

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. Find a Missing Side (Right Triangle)
    1. Identify legs and hypotenuse (hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and longest).
    2. Substitute into a2+b2=c2; solve for the unknown; simplify radicals.
  2. Use the Converse to Test for a Right Triangle
    1. Let c be the largest side.
    2. Compare a2+b2 with c2: equal → right; greater → acute; less → obtuse.
  3. Coordinate Applications
    1. Use differences in coordinates to form legs: Δx, Δy.
    2. Apply distance formula; if checking for a right angle, verify perpendicular slopes (m1m2=−1) or the converse with side lengths.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Missing Leg

Given: Right triangle with hypotenuse c=13, one leg a=5. Find: b.

  • b2=c2−a2=169−25=144 → b=12 (a 5-12-13 triple).

Example 2 — Converse Classification

Given: Sides 7, 24, 25. Decide: type of triangle.

  • 72+242=49+576=625 and 252=625 → right triangle.

Example 3 — Coordinate Distance

Find: Distance between (−3,4) and (5,−2).

  • d=(5−−3)2+(−2−4)2=82+−62=100=10.

Example 4 — Acute or Obtuse?

Given: Side lengths 9, 10, 14 (largest c=14). Classify:

  • 92+102=81+100=181, while 142=196. Since 181<196, the triangle is obtuse.

Example 5 — Exact Radical Length

Given: Leg lengths 11 and 7. Find: hypotenuse exactly.

  • c=112+72=121+49=170=√170 (already simplest radical form).

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always place the largest side as c when using the converse/inequalities.
  • Check that you actually have a right angle before applying the forward theorem to non-labeled triangles.
  • Keep subtraction order consistent for coordinate differences; negatives vanish after squaring.
  • Memorize common triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17) and scale them to save time.
  • Simplify radicals by factoring out perfect squares (e.g., 72=62).

unit: Unit 23: Trigonometric Ratios and Applications
description: Define sine, cosine, and tangent for acute angles; use trigonometric ratios to find missing sides and angles in right triangles; solve word problems involving elevation, depression, and indirect measurement.
content:
Definitions

  • Right Triangle: A triangle with one right angle (90°).
  • Reference Angle θ: An acute angle in a right triangle used to define side roles.
  • Sides (relative to θ): Opposite (across from θ), Adjacent (next to θ), and Hypotenuse (across from the right angle).
  • Trigonometric Ratios (SOH–CAH–TOA):
    • sinθ=oppositehypotenuse
    • cosθ=adjacenthypotenuse
    • tanθ=oppositeadjacent
  • Reciprocals: cscθ=1sinθ, secθ=1cosθ, cotθ=1tanθ (optional in this unit).
  • Angle of Elevation/Depression: Angle formed with the horizontal when looking up/down to an object.
  • Inverse Trig: sin−1, cos−1, tan−1 return an angle from a ratio.

Key Concepts

  • Pythagorean Theorem: For legs a, b and hypotenuse c, a2+b2=c2.
  • Choosing a Ratio: Use the sides you know and the side you need (SOH–CAH–TOA). Avoid introducing unknowns unnecessarily.
  • Inverse Trig to Find Angles: If you know two sides, find θ via θ=sin−1(opphyp), etc.
  • Scale Invariance: Trig ratios depend on angle, not on the triangle’s size.
  • Exact Values: For special angles (30°, 45°, 60°), use special right triangle ratios for exact radicals.
  • Units: Calculators must use the correct mode (degree vs. radian) to match the problem statement.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Solving Right Triangles)

  1. Label sides relative to the given/reference angle θ (opp/adj/hyp).
  2. Select a ratio (sin, cos, tan) that involves only knowns and the unknown you seek.
  3. Write an equation from the ratio and solve for the missing side or angle.
  4. Use inverse trig to find an angle from side lengths when needed.
  5. Check reasonableness: hypotenuse is longest; angles sum to 180°; units included.

Applications Procedure (Angles of Elevation/Depression)

  1. Sketch a diagram with a horizontal line and identify the angle with the horizontal.
  2. Introduce variables for unknown heights/distances; label opposite/adjacent/hypotenuse.
  3. Choose the appropriate trig ratio (often tan for height–distance problems).
  4. Solve and interpret in context; include units and, if asked, round sensibly.

Example 1 — Find a Side with Cosine

Given: In a right triangle, θ=37°, hypotenuse c=15 m. Find adjacent side a.

  • cosθ=ac → a=ccosθ=15cos(37°) ≈ 12.0 m.

Example 2 — Find an Angle with Tangent

Given: Opposite side o=7 cm, adjacent side a=10 cm. Find θ.

  • tanθ=710 → θ=tan−1(710) ≈ 34.99°.

Example 3 — Height from Angle of Elevation

Given: From a point on level ground 120 ft from a building, the angle of elevation to the top is 28°. Find the building’s height (to the top from eye level).

  • Use tangent: tan28°=height120 → height=120tan(28°) ≈ 63.8 ft.

Example 4 — Ladder Safety (Angle with Cosine)

Given: A 20-ft ladder reaches a windowsill 16 ft above the ground. What is the angle the ladder makes with the ground?

  • cosθ=adjacenthypotenuse=1620=45 → θ=cos−1(45) ≈ 36.87°.

Example 5 — Missing Side via Two Steps

Given: Right triangle with θ=55° and adjacent side a=9 m. Find the hypotenuse c and opposite side o.

  • From cosine: cos55°=9c → c=9cos55° ≈ 15.7 m.
  • Then from sine: o=csin55° ≈ 12.9 m (or via o=atan55°).

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always identify sides relative to the chosen angle; opposite/adjacent swap if you change the reference angle.
  • Use the calculator in the correct mode (DEG vs RAD). A wrong mode is a common source of error.
  • Prefer the ratio that uses only one unknown. If two sides are known, find the third with Pythagoras before/after trig as convenient.
  • For applications, draw a quick sketch and label angles with the horizontal to avoid misplacing elevation/depression.
  • Round at the end; keep intermediate values in calculator memory to reduce rounding error.

unit: Unit 24: Law of Sines and Law of Cosines
description: Apply the Law of Sines and Law of Cosines to solve oblique triangles (AAS, ASA, SSA, SAS, SSS cases); determine area of triangles using trigonometric methods; model and solve real-world problems involving non-right triangles.
content:
Unit 24: Law of Sines and Law of Cosines

Objectives

  • Solve oblique (non-right) triangles using the Law of Sines and the Law of Cosines.
  • Handle the SSA ambiguity (0–1–2 possible triangles) and validate triangle existence.
  • Compute triangle area using 12absinC and related forms.
  • Apply to word problems (navigation, surveying, bearings) and coordinate geometry.

Key Definitions

  • Oblique Triangle: A triangle with no right angle (all angles acute/obtuse).
  • Notation: Sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C, respectively.
  • Included Angle: The angle between two given sides (e.g., C is included by sides a and b).
  • Bearing: Direction measured clockwise from north; can be converted to standard angle for trigonometric modeling.

Formulas

  • Law of Sines (valid for any triangle): asinA=bsinB=csinC or in pair form asinA=bsinB, etc.
  • Law of Cosines (generalized Pythagorean):
    • a2=b2+c2−2bccosA
    • b2=a2+c2−2accosB
    • c2=a2+b2−2abcosC
  • Area of any triangle:
    • K=12absinC (and cyclic variants)
    • Heron’s Formula: K=s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c), where s=(a+b+c)2

When to Use Which Law

  • Law of Sines: ASA or AAS (always); SSA (watch ambiguity).
  • Law of Cosines: SSS (to find one angle first) or SAS (to find the unknown side opposite the included angle).

Step-by-Step Procedures

  1. ASA / AAS with Law of Sines
    1. Find the third angle using A+B+C=180°.
    2. Use a known side/angle pair in Law of Sines to solve for remaining sides.
  2. SAS with Law of Cosines
    1. Use the included angle with two known sides to compute the opposite side via Law of Cosines.
    2. Switch to Law of Sines (or Cosines) to find another angle/side.
  3. SSS with Law of Cosines
    1. Choose the largest angle (opposite the largest side) and apply Law of Cosines.
    2. Find a second angle with Law of Sines or Cosines; compute the third by angle sum.
  4. SSA Ambiguous Case (Law of Sines)
    1. Compute the altitude h=bsinA (assuming given A, a, b): compare a with h and b.
    2. If a<h: no triangle. If a=h: right triangle (one solution). If h<a<b: two triangles. If a≥b: one triangle.
    3. Use Law of Sines to find an angle; remember sin has two solutions: θ and 180°−θ; test feasibility with angle sum.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — ASA (Law of Sines)

Given: A=42°, C=68°, a=12. Find: B, b, c.

  • B=180°−42°−68°=70°.
  • Law of Sines: bsinB=asinA gives b=12sin70°/sin42°; similarly for c.

Example 2 — SAS (Law of Cosines)

Given: b=7, c=9, A=50°. Find: a.

  • a2=72+92−2(7)(9)cos50° → compute a; then use Law of Sines/Cosines for other parts.

Example 3 — SSS (Law of Cosines → Law of Sines)

Given: a=11, b=14, c=8. Find: angles.

  • Largest side is b → find B first: cosB=a2+c2−b22ac; then another angle by Law of Sines.

Example 4 — SSA Ambiguity

Given: A=38°, a=10, b=12. Find: possible B.

  • sinB=bsinA/a=12sin38°/10. If the value is ≤ 1, then B=arcsin(…) or 180°−arcsin(…).
  • Test each candidate with angle sum to see if it yields a valid positive third angle.

Example 5 — Area from Two Sides and Included Angle

Given: b=13, c=10, A=71°. Find: area K.

  • K=12bcsinA=12(13)(10)sin71°.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Match sides with their opposite angles consistently; mispairing breaks both laws.
  • After finding one angle via inverse cosine/sine, use angle sum to reduce rounding error (carry extra decimals until final answer).
  • For SSS, compute the largest angle first using Law of Cosines to avoid ambiguous sine solutions.
  • In SSA, check the altitude test (h=bsinA) to predict 0/1/2 solutions before solving.
  • Units: angles in degrees unless otherwise stated; convert to radians when required by context.

unit: Unit 25: Geometric Probability
description: Model probabilities using area and length ratios; compute likelihoods with segments, regions, and target areas; solve problems involving random points, chord/sector selections, and simulations/experimental design.
content:
Definitions

  • Geometric Probability: The probability of an event that involves a geometric measure, such as length, area, or volume, rather than counting discrete outcomes.
  • Favorable Region: The part of the geometric figure that represents successful or desired outcomes.
  • Total Region (Sample Space): The entire figure or space in which outcomes are possible.
  • Formula: P=MeasureofFavorableRegion÷MeasureofTotalRegion or simply P=favorabletotal.
  • Measure: The type of geometric quantity used — length (1D), area (2D), or volume (3D).
  • Uniform Distribution: Every location in the region has an equal chance of being selected.

Key Concepts

  • Length-Based Probability: For 1D figures such as a line segment — use P=favorablelengthsegment.
  • Area-Based Probability: For 2D figures like circles, rectangles, or polygons — use P=areafavorableregion.
  • Volume-Based Probability: For 3D solids — use P=volumefavorableregion.
  • Interpretation: A geometric probability equals the ratio of part to whole — similar to finding a fractional area or segment.
  • Uniformity: Assumes each point in the total region is equally likely to be chosen.

Step-by-Step Procedure

  1. Identify the total region and compute its measure (length, area, or volume).
  2. Define the favorable region — the set of points meeting the event condition.
  3. Compute its measure using formulas for geometric shapes (rectangle, circle, etc.).
  4. Find the ratio: P=measurefavorable/measuretotal.
  5. Convert the result to a decimal or percent, depending on context.

Example 1 — Length-Based Probability

Given: A point is chosen at random along a line segment of length 12 cm. What is the probability it lies within 4 cm of one endpoint?

  • Favorable length = 4 cm on one end + 4 cm on the other = 8 cm.
  • Total length = 12 cm.
  • P=812=23 ≈ 0.667.

Example 2 — Area-Based Probability (Circle)

Given: A dart lands randomly inside a circular target of radius 10 cm. Find the probability it lands within a bullseye of radius 3 cm.

  • Favorable area = π32 = 9π cm².
  • Total area = π102 = 100π cm².
  • P=9100 = 0.09.

Example 3 — Area Probability (Rectangle)

Given: A point is randomly chosen in a rectangle 10 m by 6 m. What is the probability it lies within a 4 m by 3 m subrectangle?

  • Favorable area = 4 × 3 = 12 m².
  • Total area = 10 × 6 = 60 m².
  • P=1260=15 = 0.20.

Example 4 — Volume-Based Probability (Sphere)

Given: A point is randomly selected inside a sphere of radius 6 cm. Find the probability that it lies within a smaller concentric sphere of radius 3 cm.

  • Favorable volume = 43π33 = 36π cm³.
  • Total volume = 43π63 = 288π cm³.
  • P=36288=18 = 0.125.

Example 5 — Conditional Area Probability

Given: A square dartboard has side 8 cm. The shaded region inside is a smaller square of side 4 cm centered in the larger one. Find the probability that a dart lands in the shaded region.

  • Favorable area = 4² = 16 cm².
  • Total area = 8² = 64 cm².
  • P=1664=14 = 0.25.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Match the type of measure (length, area, or volume) to the dimension of the problem.
  • Ensure regions are similar or comparable (e.g., both circles or both rectangles) before forming a ratio.
  • Units cancel in probability ratios — no need to convert if both measures use the same unit.
  • Do not include irrelevant or overlapping regions in total area or volume.
  • Always check that the probability lies between 0 and 1.

unit: Unit 26: Using Geometry in Real-World Contexts
description: Apply geometric reasoning to design and measurement tasks (e.g., scale drawings, blueprints, packaging, optimization); interpret tolerances and error bounds; justify assumptions and validate models with units and precision.
content:
Unit 26: Using Geometry in Real-World Contexts

Objectives

  • Translate real-world situations into geometric models (diagrams, variables, equations, and inequalities).
  • Use similarity, right-triangle trigonometry, circles, coordinate geometry, and measurement to solve applied problems.
  • Interpret results in context, including units, precision, error bounds, and reasonableness checks.

Key Definitions

  • Model: A representation of a real situation using diagrams, variables, and mathematical relationships.
  • Scale Drawing: A diagram where lengths are proportional to actual lengths by a constant scale factor.
  • Rate/Density: A ratio comparing different units (e.g., speed in m/s, population per km², material density in g/cm³).
  • Angle of Elevation/Depression: Angle measured upward/downward from the horizontal line of sight.
  • Tolerance: Allowed variation in a measurement, often expressed as ± a value or percentage.

Core Tools & Relationships

  • Similarity (AA, SAS~, SSS~) → corresponding sides in proportion; use for indirect measurement: a1a2=b1b2=c1c2.
  • Right-Triangle Trigonometry: sinθ=opphyp, cosθ=adjhyp, tanθ=oppadj.
  • Coordinate Geometry: distance, slope, and equations to represent constraints/paths; area via coordinates when needed.
  • Measurement & Units: area/volume formulas; unit conversions with dimensional analysis.
  • Optimization: choose dimensions that minimize/maximize a quantity under constraints (often perimeter/area/cost).

Modeling Process (Step-by-Step)

  1. Define the Goal: What must be found? (height, distance, cost, angle, area, etc.)
  2. Draw & Label: Sketch a diagram; mark known/unknown quantities with variables and units.
  3. Select Relationships: Choose similarity, trig, Pythagorean, circle, or coordinate formulas that fit.
  4. Form Equations: Write equations/inequalities from the relationships and constraints.
  5. Solve & Check: Compute unknowns, verify units, and test reasonableness (bounds, signs, magnitudes).
  6. Interpret: State the answer with units and appropriate precision; include tolerances if given.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Indirect Height via Shadow (Similarity)

Situation: A 1.6 m stick casts a 2.0 m shadow; a tree casts a 15.0 m shadow at the same time. Find: tree height.

  • Similar right triangles (same sun angle): 1.62.0=h15.0 → h=1.62.0·15.0=12 m.

Example 2 — Ladder Safety Angle (Trig & Clearance)

Situation: A 20 ft ladder must reach a 18 ft roof edge and meet safety rule 75°±5° with ground. Decide: feasible?

  • Height requirement: sinθ=1820=0.9 → θ=arcsin(0.9)≈64°, outside 70°–80°. Not feasible with 20 ft ladder; a longer ladder is required.

Example 3 — Fencing a Rectangular Garden (Optimization)

Situation: 120 m of fencing for a rectangle; maximize area.

  • Let length L, width W; constraint 2L+2W=120 → W=60−L. Area A = L(60−L) is maximized at a square: L=W=30, giving A=900 m².

Example 4 — Map Scale & Bearings (Scale Drawing)

Situation: Map scale 1:50,000. Town A to B measures 7.2 cm on the map along bearing 040°. Find: ground distance.

  • Actual distance: 7.2 cm × 50,000 = 360,000 cm = 3.6 km. Direction remains 040° (bearing from north).

Example 5 — Roofing Rafter Length (Coordinate/Trig)

Situation: A roof rises 4 in for every 12 in of run (pitch 4/12). Half-span from wall to ridge is 9 ft; ridge board thickness negligible. Find: rafter length.

  • Rise = 412 × 9 ft = 3 ft. Rafter is hypotenuse: ℓ=92+32=90=310 ft ≈ 9.49 ft (cut to nearest 1/8 in as needed).

Strategies & Reasonableness Checks

  • Units First: Convert all quantities to consistent units before solving; label every intermediate step.
  • Draw to Scale (when possible): A quick scale sketch helps detect impossible results (e.g., negative heights, angles too large).
  • Bounds: Compare with easy upper/lower bounds (e.g., triangle inequality, max/min angles, similar-triangle ratios).
  • Precision: Carry extra digits during calculations; round only at the end to the measurement precision given.
  • Sensitivity: For measurements with tolerance, re-compute with extremes (± tolerance) to report a realistic range.

unit: Unit 27: Coordinate Geometry in Modeling
description: Use coordinates to model and solve geometric problems: fit and analyze lines/circles, partition segments in a given ratio, optimize distances, and prove properties with vectors/slope/distance/midpoint formulas in context-rich tasks.
content:
Definitions

  • Coordinate Model: A representation of a real situation using points, equations, and inequalities in the coordinate plane.
  • Parameter: A constant in a model (e.g., slope, intercept, radius) that determines the model’s shape/position.
  • Constraint (Feasible Region): A requirement written as an inequality (or system) whose common solutions form the set of allowable points.
  • Objective (Optimization): A quantity to maximize/minimize (e.g., distance, area, cost) subject to constraints.
  • Piecewise Model: A function defined by different formulas on different intervals or regions.

Key Concepts

  • Lines as Models: Linear relationships use y=mx+b; slope m is rate of change, intercept b is starting value.
  • Distance & Midpoint: d=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2, M=(x1+x22,y1+y22).
  • Perpendicular/Parallel Conditions: Nonvertical parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular nonvertical lines satisfy m1·m2=−1.
  • Circles & Regions: Circle with center (h,k), radius r: (x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2; interior uses ≤, exterior ≥.
  • Inequality Regions: Half-planes from linear inequalities; intersections model feasible sets.
  • Area from Coordinates (Triangle): A=12|x1(y2−y3)+x2(y3−y1)+x3(y1−y2)| (shoelace for polygons generalizes).

Step-by-Step Procedure (Building a Coordinate Model)

  1. Define variables & axes: Choose what x and y represent; set units.
  2. Translate conditions into equations/inequalities (lines, circles, or systems).
  3. Identify parameters (slope, intercepts, center, radius) and compute from data.
  4. Graph/visualize the relations; shade feasible regions if constraints exist.
  5. Answer the question (predict, optimize, or verify) using algebraic or geometric reasoning.

Example 1 — Linear Model from Two Data Points

Scenario: Water depth (cm) in a tank decreases linearly from (t,d) = (0,120) to (8,72). Find d as a function of time t and predict depth at t=15 h.

  • Slope m=72−1208−0=−488 = −6 cm/h.
  • Model: d=−6t+120. At t=15: d=−90+120=30 cm.

Example 2 — Feasible Region with Linear & Circular Constraints

Scenario: A park bench must be placed inside a rectangular plaza 0≤x≤20, 0≤y≤12 but at least 3 units from a fountain centered at (8,6). Write constraints and test if (5,3) is allowed.

  • Rectangle: 0≤x≤20, 0≤y≤12.
  • Distance constraint: outside circle of radius 3 → (x−8)2+(y−6)2≥9.
  • Test (5,3): distance squared = (−3)2+(−3)2=18 ≥ 9 → allowed.

Example 3 — Shortest Path (Point to Line)

Scenario: A delivery robot at (9,2) must reach the straight conveyor line y=12x+1. Find the foot of the perpendicular (closest point) on the line.

  • Perpendicular slope is −2. Through (9,2): y−2=−2(x−9).
  • Intersect with conveyor: solve 12x+1=−2x+20 → 52x=19 → x=385, y=12·385+1=195+1=245.
  • Closest point: (385,245).

Example 4 — Area of a Lot from Survey Points

Scenario: A triangular parcel has corners A(2,1), B(9,3), C(4,8). Find the area.

  • A=12|2(3−8)+9(8−1)+4(1−3)| = 12|−10+63−8|=12·45=22.5 square units.

Example 5 — Modeling a Safety Zone with a Circle Inequality

Scenario: A drone must stay within 200 m of the base at (−1,3) and above a boundary line y=−14x+2. Write the feasible region and check if position (120,40) is valid.

  • Within circle: (x+1)2+(y−3)2≤2002.
  • Above line: y≥−14x+2.
  • Check (120,40): distance squared to base = (121)2+(37)2=14641+1369=16010 ≤ 40000 ✓; line value at x=120 is −30+2=−28, and 40≥−28 ✓ → feasible.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • State units and what each variable represents before writing equations.
  • Use inequalities to capture limits (at most/at least, inside/outside) and equalities for exact relationships.
  • Graph first for insight; then solve algebraically to confirm.
  • For “closest”/“shortest” problems, think perpendiculars or minimize distance squared to avoid square roots.
  • When computing polygon area from coordinates, keep vertex order consistent (clockwise or counterclockwise) to apply the shoelace correctly.

unit: Unit 28: Applying Trigonometric Ratios in Problem Solving
description: Model real-world and design problems using right-triangle trigonometry and inverse trig; resolve elevation/depression, bearing, and indirect measurement scenarios; incorporate error analysis and appropriate precision in solutions.
content:
Definitions

  • Trigonometric Ratios: Relationships between sides of a right triangle based on one of its acute angles. These include sine, cosine, and tangent.
  • Sine (sin): Ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse: sin=oppositehypotenuse.
  • Cosine (cos): Ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse: cos=adjacenthypotenuse.
  • Tangent (tan): Ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side: tan=oppositeadjacent.
  • Inverse Trigonometric Functions: Used to find angles when sides are known. Examples: sin−1, cos−1, tan−1.
  • Angle of Elevation: The angle formed by a horizontal line and the line of sight upward to an object.
  • Angle of Depression: The angle formed by a horizontal line and the line of sight downward to an object.

Key Formulas

  • sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse
  • cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse
  • tan θ = opposite / adjacent
  • Pythagorean Identity: sin2θ+cos2θ=1.
  • Complementary Angles: sin(90°−θ)=cosθ, tan(90°−θ)=1tanθ.

Step-by-Step Procedure (Solving Right Triangle Problems)

  1. Identify the given sides and angles in the triangle.
  2. Select the correct trigonometric ratio based on known and unknown sides.
  3. Substitute known values into the formula.
  4. Solve for the unknown side or angle using algebra or inverse trig functions.
  5. Check that answers make sense (angles sum to 180°, sides positive, hypotenuse largest).

Example 1 — Finding a Side Using Tangent

Given: A 15 ft ladder leans against a wall, making a 70° angle with the ground. Find the height of the wall it reaches.

  • Use sine: sin70°=opposite15.
  • Opposite = 15 × sin 70° ≈ 15 × 0.9397 = 14.1 ft.

Example 2 — Finding an Angle Using Tangent

Given: A ramp rises 1.5 m over a horizontal distance of 6 m. Find the angle of elevation.

  • tanθ=1.56 → θ=tan−1(0.25) ≈ 14.0°.

Example 3 — Height and Distance Problem

Given: From the top of a 50 m building, the angle of depression to a car on the ground is 35°. Find the horizontal distance to the car.

  • tan 35° = opposite / adjacent → 50 / d.
  • d = 50 / tan 35° ≈ 71.4 m.

Example 4 — Solving for Multiple Sides

Given: A right triangle has a 40° angle and hypotenuse 25 m. Find the other two sides.

  • Opposite = 25 × sin 40° = 25 × 0.6428 = 16.07 m.
  • Adjacent = 25 × cos 40° = 25 × 0.7660 = 19.15 m.

Example 5 — Application: Angle of Elevation Between Two Points

Given: You stand 40 m from the base of a tower. The angle of elevation to the top is 55°. Find the tower’s height.

  • tan55°=h40 → h = 40 × tan 55° ≈ 40 × 1.428 = 57.1 m.

Example 6 — Using Inverse Functions

Given: In a right triangle, the opposite side is 8 cm and the hypotenuse is 10 cm. Find the acute angle.

  • sinθ=810 → θ=sin−1(0.8) ≈ 53.1°.

Example 7 — Solving for Real-World Lengths Using Multiple Triangles

Scenario: A balloon is 100 m above the ground. The angle of elevation from a point A is 45°, and from a farther point B is 30°. Find the distance between A and B.

  • Let x = distance from A to balloon base. tan 45° = 100/x → x = 100.
  • Let y = distance from B to base. tan 30° = 100/y → y = 100 / 0.577 = 173.2.
  • Distance AB = 173.2 − 100 = 73.2 m.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always check which sides are known and which ratio (sin, cos, tan) fits.
  • Use degrees or radians consistently (most geometry contexts use degrees).
  • For height problems, draw a diagram showing horizontal distance and height clearly.
  • For angles of depression, the horizontal reference is from the observer’s eye level.
  • Round answers only at the end to reduce rounding error.

unit: Unit 29: Advanced Geometric Constructions and Loci
description: Use compass-and-straightedge (and dynamic geometry tools) to construct perpendicular/angle bisectors, parallel lines, equilateral triangles, and copies of segments/angles; construct triangle centers (circumcenter, incenter, centroid, orthocenter) and analyze their properties; solve locus problems describing sets of points defined by distance constraints (from a point, a line, or two points/lines) and connect loci to coordinate and algebraic representations.
content:
Definitions

  • Geometric Construction: Creating figures using only an ideal straightedge (no markings) and compass, with logical justification for each step.
  • Locus (plural: Loci): The set of all points that satisfy a given condition or rule.
  • Perpendicular Bisector: A line that is perpendicular to a segment at its midpoint; the locus of points equidistant from the segment’s endpoints.
  • Angle Bisector: A ray that divides an angle into two congruent angles; the locus of points equidistant from the angle’s sides (within the angle).
  • Circle as a Locus: The set of all points at a fixed distance r from a center O.
  • Parallel Line (through a point): A line constructed through a given point that does not intersect a given line in a plane.
  • Equidistance: A point is equidistant from objects if its distances to them are equal (e.g., to two points, or to two lines).

Key Concepts

  • Basic Loci Rules:
    • Fixed distance from a point → circle.
    • Fixed distance from a line → two parallel lines (offsets) or a single line if including both sides with absolute value.
    • Equidistant from two points → perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting them.
    • Equidistant from two intersecting lines → the pair of angle bisectors.
    • Constant sum of distances to two points → ellipse (advanced enrichment).
  • Construction Justification: Each step must be backed by a theorem/postulate (e.g., all radii in a circle are congruent; vertical angles are congruent; corresponding arcs give equal chords).
  • Concurrency Facts (for triangle centers): Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcenter; angle bisectors at the incenter; medians at the centroid; altitudes at the orthocenter (centers can be constructed via loci).
  • Intersection of Loci: Complex conditions are solved by intersecting simpler loci (solution points lie on all required loci simultaneously).

Step-by-Step Procedures (Core Constructions)

  1. Copy a Segment \(\overline{AB}\) to start at point P:
    1. Set compass to radius |AB|.
    2. Draw an arc from P to mark Q; then ∠QP=|AB| gives PQ=AB.
  2. Copy an Angle \(\angle ABC\) at point P:
    1. Same-radius arc across both rays of \(\angle ABC\) to create chordal marks.
    2. Replicate arc at P; transfer the chord distance with the compass to locate the second ray.
  3. Perpendicular Bisector of segment \(\overline{AB}\):
    1. With a radius > half of AB, draw arcs centered at A and B on both sides of the segment.
    2. Connect arc intersections; this line is perpendicular to and bisects \(\overline{AB}\).
  4. Angle Bisector of \(\angle ABC\):
    1. Arc centered at B meets both sides at E and F.
    2. Equal-radius arcs from E and F intersect at G; line BG bisects the angle.
  5. Parallel Through a Point (Thales/alt. interior):
    1. Copy the corresponding angle of line ℓ at external point P to create a line parallel to ℓ.
  6. Perpendicular Through a Point to line ℓ:
    1. If point on the line: construct isosceles triangles with equal arcs to locate the perpendicular.
    2. If point off the line: use circle intersections to form a right triangle whose hypotenuse midpoint lies on the perpendicular.

Loci Procedures

  1. Translate the condition into an equidistance statement or fixed distance.
  2. Name the simple locus (circle, parallel offsets, perpendicular bisector, angle bisector).
  3. Intersect loci if multiple conditions are required; justify that intersection points satisfy all conditions.

Example 1 — Locus Equidistant from Two Towns

Given: Towns at points A and B. Find possible locations for a service center equidistant from both.

  • The locus is the perpendicular bisector of AB. Any point on it satisfies PA=PB.

Example 2 — Locus at Fixed Distance from a Road

Given: A road is modeled by line r. A walking path must be exactly 30 m from the road.

  • The locus is the pair of lines parallel to r at distance 30 m on each side.

Example 3 — Incenter via Loci

Given: Triangle △ABC. Locate the point equidistant from all three sides.

  • Intersect the three angle bisectors. Their concurrency point is the incenter, locus of points equidistant from each side; it is the center of the incircle.

Example 4 — Circumcenter via Loci

Given: Triangle △ABC. Locate the point equidistant from the vertices.

  • Intersect the perpendicular bisectors of two sides; the point is the circumcenter, center of the circumscribed circle through A, B, C.

Example 5 — Intersection of Two Loci (Placement Problem)

Problem: Place a sensor P that is 5 m from point S and equidistant from lines ℓ and m (intersecting). Find all possible locations.

  • Locus 1: Circle C with center S and radius 5.
  • Locus 2: The angle bisectors of ℓ and m (two lines).
  • Solutions: intersection points of circle C with each angle bisector (0–4 points depending on configuration).

Example 6 — Constructing a Regular Hexagon (Advanced)

Goal: Construct a regular hexagon inscribed in a given circle with center O.

  • Pick a point A on the circle; set compass radius to OA (the circle’s radius).
  • Step off six equal arcs around the circle to get vertices; connect consecutively to form the hexagon (chords equal to the radius).

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Do not change compass width mid-step unless a step requires it; mark settings lightly.
  • Justify each step with a theorem (e.g., equal radii in a circle, properties of perpendicular/angle bisectors).
  • Check locus domains: Angle-bisector locus applies inside the angle unless stated otherwise.
  • Use intersections to satisfy multiple conditions; be mindful of extraneous branches of a locus.
  • Label cleanly and keep construction lines/arcs visible until the proof/argument is complete.

unit: Unit 30: Foundations of Non-Euclidean and Spherical Geometry
description: Compare Euclid’s Parallel Postulate with alternatives; examine models of non-Euclidean geometry qualitatively (Poincaré disk/upper half-plane) and spherical geometry (great circles as geodesics, triangle angle sum > 180°, spherical polygons); explore real-world applications such as navigation and map projections, emphasizing similarities/differences from Euclidean results.
content:
Unit 30: Foundations of Non-Euclidean and Spherical Geometry

Objectives

  • Understand the fundamental assumptions (postulates) of Euclidean geometry and how altering them leads to non-Euclidean systems.
  • Explore the geometry of curved surfaces, particularly spherical geometry, and compare its principles to the Euclidean plane.
  • Analyze real-world applications of non-Euclidean geometry in astronomy, navigation, and physics (general relativity).

Foundational Concepts

  • Euclidean Geometry: Based on Euclid’s five postulates, including the Parallel Postulate: through a point not on a line, exactly one line can be drawn parallel to the given line.
  • Non-Euclidean Geometry: Geometric systems developed when the Parallel Postulate is replaced or modified. Two major types:
    • Hyperbolic Geometry: Through a point not on a line, infinitely many lines can be drawn parallel to the given line.
    • Elliptic (Spherical) Geometry: Through a point not on a line, no parallel lines exist—great circles always intersect.
  • Plane vs. Surface Geometry: Euclidean geometry occurs on a flat plane, while spherical geometry takes place on the surface of a sphere.
  • Great Circle: The largest possible circle on a sphere, formed by intersecting the sphere with a plane through its center (e.g., Earth's equator, meridians).

Key Properties — Spherical vs. Euclidean Geometry

PropertyEuclidean GeometrySpherical Geometry
LinesInfinite straight pathsGreat circles (finite, but unbounded)
Parallel LinesCan exist; one unique parallel through a pointNo parallels; all great circles intersect
Angle Sum of TriangleExactly 180°Greater than 180° (depends on triangle area)
Similar TrianglesPossible without congruenceAll similar triangles are congruent
Shortest PathStraight lineArc of a great circle

Formulas & Relationships

  • Spherical Excess: For a triangle on a sphere of radius r with angles A, B, C: E=A+B+C−180°. The area of the spherical triangle is A=E·π180·r2.
  • Arc Length: s=rθ (with θ in radians).
  • Surface Distance on Earth: d=rΔσ, where Δσ is the central angle between two points (radians).
  • Spherical Law of Cosines: cosa=cosbcosc+sinbsinccosA.

Step-by-Step Reasoning

  1. Identify the Surface Type: Determine if the problem is planar (flat) or spherical (curved surface).
  2. Draw a Diagram: Represent the geometry with labeled points, arcs, and relevant great circles.
  3. Choose the Appropriate Model:
    • Flat distances/angles → Euclidean postulates.
    • Large-scale navigation/planetary motion → spherical or non-Euclidean formulas.
  4. Apply Relationships:
    • Use Euclidean or spherical laws of sines/cosines as needed.
    • Check consistency with expected properties (sum of triangle angles, curvature, etc.).
  5. Interpret in Context: Convert angular measures to physical distances; verify results align with curvature and real-world units.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Comparing Triangle Angle Sums

Situation: On a flat plane, A+B+C=180°. On Earth, a triangle formed by the equator and two meridians 90° apart meets at the North Pole.

  • Each vertex at the pole measures 90°; thus the triangle’s angle sum = 270° → spherical excess 90°.
  • The triangle covers one-eighth of Earth’s surface (since 360° / 4 = 90°).

Example 2 — Great-Circle Distance

Given: Two cities at latitude 40°N, longitudes 75°W and 120°W. Find: Distance along Earth’s surface (r=6371 km).

  • Central angle Δσ=Δλcosφ=(45°)cos40°≈34.5° = 0.602 rad.
  • d=6371×0.602≈3835 km.

Example 3 — Hyperbolic Contrast

Idea: In hyperbolic geometry (saddle-shaped space), triangle angle sums are less than 180°. Distances grow exponentially with coordinate differences, modeled using negative curvature K<0.

  • Real-world analogs include models in relativity and certain optical surfaces.

Applications

  • Navigation & Astronomy: Great-circle routes for aircraft and ships minimize distance over Earth’s curved surface.
  • Geodesy: Measuring and modeling Earth's shape and curvature for mapping and GPS accuracy.
  • Physics: Einstein’s theory of general relativity uses non-Euclidean geometry to describe spacetime curvature near massive bodies.
  • Art & Design: Tessellations on spheres (e.g., soccer balls, geodesic domes) apply spherical symmetry principles.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Always specify whether distances are measured on the surface (curved) or in space (straight-line chord).
  • For small triangles (local scales), spherical geometry approximates Euclidean closely.
  • Do not assume parallel lines exist on a sphere—great circles always meet.
  • When using spherical trigonometry, convert all angles to radians before applying formulas.
  • Check for over-rounding; small angular errors can produce large surface distance changes.

unit: Unit 31: Solid Geometry, Cross-Sections, and Spatial Visualization
description: Analyze 3D figures (prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones, spheres) using nets, surface development, and Euler’s formula (V − E + F = 2) for polyhedra; determine and sketch cross-sections of solids and identify resulting 2D figures; relate solids of revolution (qualitatively) and use coordinate/vector methods to compute distances and interpret spatial relationships in modeling tasks.
content:
Definitions

  • Solid Geometry: The study of three-dimensional (3D) figures, including their surfaces, volumes, and cross-sections.
  • Polyhedron: A solid bounded by flat polygonal faces, straight edges, and vertices (e.g., prisms, pyramids).
  • Non-Polyhedron: Solids with curved surfaces (e.g., cylinders, cones, spheres).
  • Cross-Section: The two-dimensional shape formed when a solid is cut by a plane.
  • Spatial Visualization: The ability to mentally picture and manipulate 3D objects from different perspectives or sections.
  • Net: A two-dimensional figure that can be folded to form a 3D solid.
  • Oblique vs. Right Solid: A right solid has lateral edges perpendicular to the base; an oblique solid does not.

Key Concepts

  • Prisms: Two congruent, parallel polygonal bases connected by rectangular (lateral) faces. Volume V=Bh, where B = base area.
  • Pyramids: One polygonal base and triangular lateral faces meeting at a vertex. Volume V=13Bh.
  • Cylinder: Two congruent, parallel circular bases; V=πrr2h.
  • Cone: One circular base with a vertex; V=13πrr2h.
  • Sphere: All points in space equidistant from a center; V=43πrr3.
  • Euler’s Formula: For convex polyhedra, V−E+F=2 (vertices, edges, faces).

Types of Cross-Sections

  • Prisms: Horizontal cut → same shape as base; diagonal cut → parallelogram.
  • Pyramids: Parallel to base → similar (smaller) polygon; slanted cut → trapezoid or triangle.
  • Cylinders: Parallel to base → circle; diagonal cut → ellipse; perpendicular through axis → rectangle.
  • Cones: Parallel to base → circle; slanted cut → ellipse/parabola/hyperbola (conic sections).
  • Spheres: Any plane cut → circle; diameter cut → great circle.

Step-by-Step Procedures (Cross-Section Analysis)

  1. Identify the solid (prism, pyramid, cone, cylinder, or sphere).
  2. Determine the orientation of the cutting plane (parallel, perpendicular, or diagonal to the base).
  3. Visualize the intersection — use nets or transparent models if needed.
  4. Name the resulting shape (circle, rectangle, trapezoid, etc.) and describe its dimensions relative to the solid.
  5. Relate 2D and 3D measures: Use area of cross-section × height for volume comparisons or ratios.

Example 1 — Prism Cross-Section

Given: A rectangular prism with base 8 × 4 and height 6 is cut by a plane parallel to the base. Find the cross-section’s area.

  • Parallel to base → cross-section congruent to base.
  • Area = 8 × 4 = 32 square units.

Example 2 — Pyramid Cross-Section

Given: A square pyramid with base side 12 and height 9 is cut by a plane parallel to the base halfway up. Find side length of cross-section.

  • Ratios of similarity: side ∝ height → s12=4.59 → s=6.
  • Cross-section: smaller square, area = 6² = 36 square units.

Example 3 — Cylinder Cross-Section

Given: A cylinder has radius 5 cm and height 10 cm. A plane cuts it perpendicular to its base. What is the cross-section shape and area?

  • Perpendicular cut → rectangle.
  • Dimensions: height 10, width = diameter = 10 → area = 100 cm².

Example 4 — Sphere Cross-Section

Given: A sphere has radius 10 cm. A plane cuts it 6 cm from the center. Find the radius of the circular cross-section.

  • Using Pythagoras: r2=102−62 → r=64=8 cm.

Example 5 — Spatial Visualization

Scenario: A cube is cut diagonally from one vertex to the opposite vertex on the far face. What is the cross-section?

  • The resulting section is a regular hexagon — slicing diagonally through opposite vertices exposes all six square faces in section.

Example 6 — Net Interpretation

Scenario: A cylinder’s net consists of two circles and a rectangle. If the cylinder’s height is 8 cm and radius 3 cm, find the rectangle’s dimensions.

  • Height = 8 cm, length = circumference of base = 2πr = 6π cm.
  • Rectangle: 6π × 8 cm.

Example 7 — Combining Solids

Given: A hemisphere of radius 4 cm is attached to a right cylinder of the same radius and height 10 cm. Find total volume.

  • Cylinder: V=πr2h=π·42·10=160π.
  • Hemisphere: V=23π43=1283π.
  • Total volume ≈ 160π+42.67π=202.67π cm³.

Quick Tips & Common Pitfalls

  • Sketch lightly in 3D; trace edges that are visible and use dashed lines for hidden ones.
  • Cross-sections parallel to bases are similar to the base; diagonal cuts often form new polygons (trapezoids, parallelograms).
  • When using nets, verify that all faces correspond to the 3D solid’s structure and dimensions.
  • Use right triangle relationships for sphere and cone cross-sections.
  • Euler’s formula applies only to convex polyhedra, not curved solids.
